document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 9(1)-(9) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Risk management system
recorded_responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
recorded_applicability: High-risk AI systems (classified under Art. 6 and Annexes I/III). Risks covered are limited to those that can be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through development, design or adequate technical information (Art. 9(3)). Art. 9(9) requires consideration of impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups.
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).
provision_summary_from_dataset: Providers must run a documented, continuous and iterative risk management process across the whole lifecycle of a high-risk AI system. It covers identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating risks from post-market monitoring data, and adopting targeted mitigation measures so that residual risk is judged acceptable. Systems must be tested, including before being placed on the market, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds (Art. 9(6)-(8)). Providers must consider likely adverse impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

article_or_section: Article 10(1)-(4), (6) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Data and data governance; read with Article 4a(1)
recorded_responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
recorded_applicability: High-risk AI systems that use techniques involving the training of AI models with data. For high-risk systems not using such training techniques, paras 2, 3 and 4 and Art. 4a(1) apply only to testing data sets (Art. 10(6) as amended).

provision_summary_from_dataset: High-risk AI systems trained on data must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet quality criteria. article_or_section: Article 13(1)-(3) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Transparency and provision of information to deployers
recorded_responsible_party: AI provider (information duty owed to deployers)
recorded_applicability: High-risk AI systems. The beneficiary of the information is the deployer, not end-users or affected persons. Transparency towards natural persons interacting with AI systems (e.g. chatbots, deepfakes) is a separate regime under Art. 50. Affected persons have a separate right to obtain explanations of individual decisions from the deployer (Art. 86, OJ p. 110).
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106). Deployers must use systems in accordance with the instructions for use (Art. 26(1); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37), with deployer breaches finable under Art. 99(4)(e).
provision_summary_from_dataset: High-risk AI systems must be transparent enough for deployers to interpret their outputs and use them appropriately. They must come with instructions for use giving concise, complete, correct and clear information. At minimum this includes the provider's identity, the system's intended purpose, its capabilities and limitations, its accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risk circumstances, any capabilities for explaining outputs, human oversight measures, maintenance needs and log-handling mechanisms.

article_or_section: Article 14(1)-(4) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Human oversight
recorded_responsible_party: AI provider (design obligation); AI deployer (implementation, via Art. 26(2))
recorded_applicability: High-risk AI systems. Additional two-person verification rule for remote biometric identification systems (Annex III point 1(a)), with an exception for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law deems it disproportionate (Art. 14(5)).
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106). Deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Art. 26(2); Art. 26 begins cons. p. 37, OJ p. 68 for para. 2; unchanged by 2026/1744); breach finable under Art. 99(4)(e).
provision_summary_from_dataset: High-risk AI systems must be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Oversight measures must be proportionate to risk, autonomy and context, and may be built in by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement. The system must be provided to the deployer so that the people assigned to oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to understand its capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, interpret its outputs, decide not to use or to override an output, and stop the system safely (Art. 14(4)).

article_or_section: Article 15(1), (3)-(5) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
recorded_responsible_party: AI provider (of high-risk AI systems)
recorded_applicability: High-risk AI systems. The feedback-loop requirement (Art. 15(4), third subpara.) applies only to systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service.
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: Art. 16(a) (cons. p. 28; OJ p. 62) obliges providers to ensure compliance with Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 8-15). Non-compliance with Art. 16 provider obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(a), cons. p. 116; OJ p. 115; unchanged by 2026/1744). For SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two applies (Art. 99(6), OJ p. 116). The Act sets maxima; Member States lay down the penalty rules and enforce them (Art. 99(1), OJ p. 115). Ex ante conformity assessment (Art. 43, cons. p. 53; OJ p. 78); market surveillance (Art. 74, cons. p. 91; OJ p. 102) and procedure for AI systems presenting a risk (Art. 79, cons. p. 104; OJ p. 106).
provision_summary_from_dataset: High-risk AI systems must achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and keep performing consistently throughout their lifecycle. They must be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies (possibly through redundancy or fail-safe plans), manage feedback loops in systems that keep learning, and resist attacks that exploit vulnerabilities. This includes, where appropriate, measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. Accuracy levels and metrics must be declared in the instructions for use.

article_or_section: Part 4 – Practical Guidelines for Industry & Regulators; 'Guidelines for industry', bullet 5 (transparency reports)
recorded_responsible_party: Developer and deployer ('any person involved in developing or deploying AI systems in India')
recorded_applicability: All developers and deployers of AI systems in India; no risk threshold or system category is defined. Elsewhere the Guidelines say that low-risk applications may need only basic commitments such as transparency reporting, while high-risk applications in sensitive sectors may need more (§2.4, PDF p. 30).
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision. The Guidelines rely on soft accountability mechanisms (public and peer scrutiny of transparency reports, self-certifications, internal policies, committee hearings, §2.5, PDF p. 33; peer monitoring and third-party audits, §2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). MeitY 'may publish a schedule' for compliance with these measures within 9-12 months (PDF p. 33). Voluntary measures may later become mandatory baseline requirements enforced by regulators (§2.4, PDF p. 29).
provision_summary_from_dataset: Anyone developing or deploying AI systems in India is advised to publish transparency reports that assess the risk of harm their systems pose to individuals and society in the Indian context. Where a report contains sensitive or proprietary information, it should be shared confidentially with the relevant regulators instead of published.

article_or_section: Part 2, §2.5 Accountability – Recommendations, bullet 2 (proportionate obligations across the AI value chain); read with 'Liability' (graded liability)
recorded_responsible_party: Government (MeitY and sectoral regulators) to clarify and impose obligations; the eventual duty-bearers would be developers, deployers and end-users
recorded_applicability: All entities in the AI value chain (developers, deployers, end-users). Obligations are to be scaled to function and risk; no thresholds are specified yet.
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: No specific mechanism identified in the examined provision; the obligations themselves do not yet exist. Enforcement of existing laws is to be 'timely and consistent' (§2.5 Recommendations, PDF p. 35). Part 3 Action Plan lists 'Develop clear liability regimes across the AI value chain' as a short-term action (PDF p. 40).
provision_summary_from_dataset: The Guidelines recommend clarifying how each actor in the AI value chain (developers, deployers, end-users) is governed under existing law such as the IT Act, and then imposing obligations on each that match its function and the risk of harm (for example transparency reporting, content removal, grievance redressal and legal assistance). This rests on a 'graded liability' model in which responsibility depends on the function performed, the level of risk and whether due diligence was done.

article_or_section: Part 2, §2.4 Risk Mitigation – Recommendations, bullet 1 (India-specific risk assessment and classification framework)
recorded_responsible_party: Government (developing body not named in the provision; Action Plan says 'with sectoral inputs'; AISI's listed functions include risk analysis)
recorded_applicability: Economy-wide framework; it would determine which AI systems need which mitigation measures. No system categories exist yet.
recorded_enforcement_mechanism: Not applicable: this is a framework-building task, not a compliance duty. The linked AI incidents database (recommendation 2, PDF p. 32) is designed to encourage reporting 'without the threat of penalties' (PDF p. 29) and would feed evidence into the framework.
provision_summary_from_dataset: The Guidelines recommend developing an India-specific framework for assessing and classifying AI risks, based on real-world evidence of harm and reflecting India's social, economic and cultural context, including risks to vulnerable groups such as children and women. Risk mitigation measures would then be applied on the basis of that classification. The Guidelines identify six risk categories: malicious use, bias and discrimination, transparency failures, systemic risks, loss of control, and national security.

recorded_enforcement_mechanism: Existing statutory powers of sectoral regulators under their own laws; no new AI-specific sanctions or enforcement powers are created. provision_summary_from_dataset: Enforcement is left to existing sectoral agencies and regulators, each within its own domain; for example, the Ministry of Finance and RBI for financial services. MeitY is the nodal ministry for AI adoption and regulation. A new AI Governance Group (AIGG), supported by a Technology & Policy Expert Committee (TPEC), is to coordinate policy across ministries, but it is a coordinating body, not an enforcement authority.
